utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This morning and continuing through this week we will be receiving testimony via video conferencing equipment from the former Yugoslavia. The Defence will be calling witnesses -- are you ready to proceed, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The first witness we call by video link is Zeljko Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro, can you hear me? Mr. Marro, the first witness the Defence calls is Mr. Zeljko Maric. He is listed as No. 33 on the Defence witness list. The last name is spelt -- yes, we are ready -- Zeljko M-A-R-I-C. Would you please ask that he come in? Mr. Marro, would you please administer the oath to Mr. Maric? ^^ ZELJKO MARIC, called

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maric, you may be seated. Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Zeljko Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In translation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you work as a policeman in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you a married man with two children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first start to work as a policeman in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are still in that occupation as a regular police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which part of the police do you work in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have received a dark signal now. The video is quashed. So we need to stop -- here, it has come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will repeat the last question again. [To the witness]: In which part of the police force do you work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long have you known Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Dusko Tadic since 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you meet Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During performing my regular duties, during traffic control and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you train at karate with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was taught by our common friend, Emir Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How well did you know Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite well, because we completed secondary school together at the Police Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your duties as a traffic policeman take you on occasions to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know a lot of people in the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when the conflict started in 1992 in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was around the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever worked with Dusko Tadic as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry. The interpreter could not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. Have you ever worked with Dusko Tadic as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the checkpoint in Orlovci I did work with Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that before or after the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after the conflict in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect with whom Dusko Tadic worked when he was at the checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In his shift there were also Cvijic -- I cannot remember the names now, perhaps later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time did you ever work on any shifts at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that on the same shift as Dusko Tadic or a different shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes we worked in the same shift, but most frequently we did not work together. He was the shift either before mine or after mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in any position of command in relation to checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, shall we say, the leader of the shift, but I do not think that can be called a command position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect for how long Dusko Tadic worked at checkpoint Orlovci? I will repeat that question, your Honour. Can you recollect for how long Dusko Tadic worked at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think around two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time Dusko Tadic worked at checkpoint Orlovci, do you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever spend any time off duty with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever spend time talking to him whilst you were both working together or on police duty with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How would you describe Dusko Tadic's behaviour during that period of time that you came across him at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He behaved quite normally, like most people at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss events that were happening at that time with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he ever express any extreme nationalist views to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he ever express nationalist views in support of the Serbs against other ethnic groups in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you discuss those sorts of matters, what was happening at that time, with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of attitude would you say Dusko Tadic had to those matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was in the first place a sportsman, so that most of the time we spent discussing sports and people in sports, but it was inevitable to touch on politics as well and the events that had taken place there at that time. I conclude from all our talks that Dusko Tadic condemned everything that was happening, including the war and everything that was happening to the people in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him what had happened to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was his attitude about the state of Kozarac, about what had happened to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac is his place of birth which means that he loves it, and that is why he denounced the way that things had happened and what had happened in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were on a different shift to Dusko Tadic, did you ever speak to each other at the handover of one shift to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, frequently I would be handing over my shift to him or the other way round and waiting for transportation, or on some other occasions we would sit and talk about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you identify for us where checkpoint Orlovci is in relation to Prijedor and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about halfway between Kozarac and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there a particular town or village at the site of the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the village is called Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it just called "Orlovci" or is it prefixed with "Donji" or "Gornji"?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The monitor has gone blank again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will repeat the question when we get back on. It does seem the quality is improving as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it just called "Orlovci" or is it prefixed with "Donji" or "Gornji"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is called "Gornji Orlovci".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the site, checkpoint, are there houses on either side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Kozarac there are more houses on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it on the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway or what is known as the old Banja Luka/Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is -- that is the place where the two roads, the old and the new one, intersect, the Banja Luka/Prijedor roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is the place of the checkpoint actually sited on the new road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are there roads to houses on either side, small lanes that move up to Gornji Orlovci on one side and down on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there still a checkpoint to this day, although not in the same form but a place where the police often stand by a vehicle on the side of the road to observe traffic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the checkpoint in the sense it used to be no longer exists, but the road is there, and the police is performing its normal duties, both there and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the site of this checkpoint, is there a large tree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a walnut tree there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you were approaching Prijedor from Kozarac, would that be on the right-hand side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In 1992 can you describe what form the checkpoint took at this place in the road, how it was set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you thinking of our duties or the actual buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The actual buildings, was it a barrier, was there some other form of causing the traffic to slow down? Can you describe how the point was set up in the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Kozarac towards Prijedor, on the right-hand side there was a container in which the policemen were accommodated and on the road itself there were signs of warning and speed reduction, so that vehicles and drivers moving along the Prijedor/Banka Luka road could easily be stopped and checked, both vehicles, drivers and the goods, and these buildings were easily visible. At night there was a lamp. There were signs of warning posted there and other necessary signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said a container was by the side of the road. Can you tell us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A container is actually a prefabricated edifice about four metres long and two metres wide, similar to those being used today by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that the container is no longer there today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will repeat that question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that the container is no longer there today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. It is no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the container was taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the container was there before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was placed there when the checkpoint was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this just a police checkpoint or was there also a military presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were members of the military police present also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they also operate on a shift system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many members of the military police would make up each shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they have the same shift patterns as the civil police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many people were in your Unit when you were on duty at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently there were four men, sometimes less, sometimes more, but most frequently there were four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were on duty at this checkpoint, were all the police that you were on duty with armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What type of weapons would they be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had pistols and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were those weapons issued by the police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are our weapons belonging to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any other checkpoints beyond Orlovci as you travelled towards Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the period we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The period I am asking you about is June and July 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was another checkpoint just before reaching Kozarac, but it was smaller and it was of short duration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that checkpoint still in place after the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was there for a very short period and then it was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when it was abolished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your work at checkpoint Orlovci come under the traffic police department of Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, we checked drivers, vehicles and goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the name of your Commander for the traffic police at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duro Tupic (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think that is "Prpos", your Honour. Is he still the Commander of the traffic police today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did he cease to be the Commander of the traffic police? When did Djuro Prpos cease to become the Commander of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, because since then two or three Commanders have changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of Commander was Djuro Prpos like in June and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question, but he was a professional Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he vigilant as to the duties of the officers who worked under him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he check that you were performing your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would come to check our duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To check your duties, did that mean to check that everyone was present who should have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he like the men who served under him to be in proper discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he required discipline ---- (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will repeat the last question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I will repeat the last question again. Can you tell the Court what the approach was of Djuro Prpos to discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He required his subordinates to act in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would he have tolerated any of his policemen being drunk on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would he have tolerated any of his policemen going absent from their posts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask my friend not lead these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think it is a leading question, your Honour, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it suggest an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness can say "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "Yes" or "no". OK. Try not to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. [To the witness]: Would he have tolerated any of his policemen not being at their posts when they were meant to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our absence was allowed only during breakfast or at meal time, so that we were obliged to be on duty at our post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far the camp of Omarska would have been if you had travelled in a vehicle from checkpoint Orlovci to the camp at Omarska at that time in June or July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By car it would take roughly between 30 and 45 minutes to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In June or July 1992 were the conditions of the roads better or worse than they are today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they worse because of the events that had taken place at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss Emir Karabasic with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were those discussions about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that both of them were sportsmen. They liked karate. Dusko used to train Emir and our talks were related to their joint successes or failures, sports competitions. They were friends there, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After Dusko Tadic ceased to work at checkpoint Orlovci, did you come across him in any of his later positions or jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that after starting to work at Orlovci that he was employed or he did something at the local community, Mesna Zajednica, in Kozarac. So he would often travel from Kozarac to Prijedor, so he would go through the checkpoint Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you continue working then at checkpoint Orlovci after Dusko Tadic had ceased his duties there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long did you continue to work at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think until 1995, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will ask the question again. When did you cease to work at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1994, '95, I could not say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask, but wait there. There will be further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, please, your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stojan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your mother's name?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am afraid we could not hear that name. Could you repeat it for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mira.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a brother and I have a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said you live in Prijedor. Do you live in the town of Prijedor or do you live out of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far out of the town of Prijedor do you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance is about three and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In what direction is that place where you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The direction of the old part of the Prijedor/Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live at this address in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the village or the nearest village to where you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The place where I live is called Donji Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you living in Donji Orlovci in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were working as a traffic policeman in 1992, what was your dress code? What uniform did you wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992 the police uniform was the one that we had before the war, and then we got the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you get the camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was in June or July, that period, I think. I cannot remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of having an automatic weapon. Were you also issued with a pistol and a knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a pistol and an automatic rifle, but I did not have a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of checking vehicles and the people that were travelling in them. What were you looking for when you stopped the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would ask them for their driver's licence and for the licence of the vehicle itself, and we would also ask for an ID for the passengers and the drivers and also for the freight, if they had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dealing first with the people, what would happen if people produced this identification and you checked it? What were you looking for precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you found a person in a vehicle, his identification showed that they come from the local area and that they were a Serb, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. If everything was normal, we would let people continue to drive wherever they were going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you consider to be abnormal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that emphasis was laid on traffic subject matters, that is, drivers, whether they had driver's licences or not, and the vehicle itself, was it technically in a good shape and whether they had the proper documents and if they were carrying freight whether they had the appropriate documents. So that is the subject matter the traffic police deals with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By "freight" do you mean commercial freight or did you look at people's personal possessions as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant commercial freight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were not interested in, for example, weapons or ammunition if that was in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the military police who were involved in that, but it was not unusual at that time for people to carry weapons from the front line or from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In July 1992, if you found a Muslim driving a vehicle with a weapon in the vehicle, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the military police who were in charge, so we would hand them over to the military police but there were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them once you handed them over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think he said there were no such cases, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. What were you told to do if you found Muslims with weapons driving motor vehicles that come past your checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tell you, it was the military police that was in charge. So such persons would be handed over to the military police, but we did not have such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what the military police would have done with them if you had found somebody with a vehicle with a Muslim in it who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would probably question him to see where they got the weapons from, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the conflict, did you perform patrols as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Our traffic police station was in charge of the wider area, so we also did that in Kozarac too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do this work alone or with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most often we would have two of us in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you operate only from a vehicle or did you also operate from fixed positions on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question or, rather, I did not hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will repeat the question for you. Did you only operate out of your police vehicle or did you operate also from fixed positions or control points on roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, the traffic police carried out their duties in terms of speed limits too, that is to say, we worked with radars. We would stand at positions where exceeding the speed limit would jeopardise traffic, so then we would check vehicles and persons driving them -- everything that was within our jurisdiction, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But would you do this only when you were operating out of your police vehicle or was there fixed control points like the one at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certain positions but they were not fixed. There were not positions where you had to be. There was not a plan of that sort. The plan would be worked out in accordance to things that were actually taking place, traffic accidents, pedestrians, the time of the day, the way in which this happened. That is why we would take a certain position so that we would prevent anything bad from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dule Tadic in Prijedor before 22nd May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you see him, and if you cannot be precise, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say that Dule Tadic was then just a normal person like anybody else. Nobody really paid special attention to him. So I would not really have to remember everything in connection with him. So I saw him in '91 or '90 perhaps. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him in the early part of 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw him in Prijedor where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In passing, simply in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were on checkpoint at Orlovci in June/July 1992, occasionally you would go away to the local houses, would you not, and have coffee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely. It happened rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You would go home for lunch, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was a restaurant near the checkpoint where we would go for a brief meal, and during a certain period of time we even had food brought to us to the checkpoint, so there was not any need for us to leave the checkpoint itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that during the conflict the police acted normally. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our regular police duties, that is to say, traffic control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But what you were doing at Orlovci was different to what you did during peace time or before 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the war everything is different from what it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So they were not acting normally then during the war? Did you hear my last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Never mind. How often did you work with Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was seldom, we would be on the same shift, I mean. That would happen rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You cannot help us at all with the dates that you worked with Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You cannot tell us whether it was early June, late June, early July, late July, mid June, mid July, something like that, you cannot help us that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You worked with him on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you know who was on Dule's shift, that is, on the occasions when you were not on his shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I would see these people during shift handover.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of the Commanders of the traffic police since Prpos was the Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Obrad Despotovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is he the only one you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that there were other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember any of their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jankovic. I think there were not any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you worked on the shift at Orlovci with Dule Tadic, do you remember whether it was day-shift or night-shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a cycle. You did not only have day-shifts or night-shifts, so you would go through an entire circle. People would work for 12 hours and then you would rest for 24 hours, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether when you worked with Dule, or can you remember when you worked with Dule Tadic, it was the day-shift or the night-shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that once we were on the day-shift and once in the night-shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you finished your shift you went home, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends at what time it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? When did you not go home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were points in time when we would not go home, when we were supposed to go to the police station to see whether there other tasks and duties awaiting us, and there were other times when we would normally go home after our shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The other tasks or duty that you had to perform that were awaiting you, what were those types of duties? Can you describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The traffic police had checkpoints, so one of these checkpoints was Orlovci, and it would happen that sometimes some of the policemen would not come to work on time and then others would have to carry out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went home were you ever called up to go back on duty after you had gone home for your two days off, your 24 hours off -- sorry, your 24 hours off?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have not got a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What happened, it would happen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ask the witness. Witness, would you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often did it happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the procedure for changing shifts? How was this done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would come to do my shift. I would get a report from my colleague who had worked previously. He would say what happened during his shift, what I should pay attention to, whether the inventory was in order, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, when you reported for duty, you were told when your next duty was, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said sometimes you were told to pay attention to certain matters. During that period, June/July 1992, can you remember whether you were requested to pay attention to anything in particular that you can bring to mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, of course, the police carries out its regular duties and tasks. However, if we are talking about extraordinary tasks, then we are told what to do by telegram -- extraordinary tasks and duties, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the extraordinary tasks and duties were during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of Dule Tadic being interested in sports. What kind of competitions did Dule Tadic engage in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule was the trainer of the sports club for karate from Kozarac and he would take his sportsmen to various competitions to different parts of Yugoslavia. I remember once he went to the seaside, to Budva, I think, when my friend Karabasic injured his foot at that competition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know when ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, I think it was in '82 or '83, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you ever recall him taking sportsmen outside of Yugoslavia or is your recollection only of events or competitions taking place within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember any competition outside Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever read newspaper articles about his sporting achievements or his involvement in sports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. All the information about sports I received from Karabasic. He informed me about the progress he made, the belts he won and the sporting activities and I enjoyed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You suggested that Dule Tadic was not a nationalist. Are you suggesting he was not particularly interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was not interested in politics or, rather, when we got together, when we talked also before the war, he never mentioned politics. He was a man linked to sports. He loved sports. He loved the youth. He liked a sporting life. He sought his team to be as successful as possible, and I just cannot understand that he could be a nationalist because he lived in Kozarac where the majority of the population were Muslims. So that if he was a nationalist, he would not have led the youth in the way he did. He would not have been so active in sports. I just cannot accept that he could be a nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know that he was one of the first members of the SDS party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard this before and I cannot recollect any evidence. I have heard Mr. Niemann say it, certainly, but I have not heard any evidence to support this information.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought Mrs. Tadic testified -- in Prijedor or Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is in an Exhibit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have the information? But Kozarac was the particular place, but it did not have a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Exhibit 344, your Honour. Perhaps it might be shown to my friend and if he cares to look at page ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The witness would not have that Exhibit. Maybe you can take a look at it, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not know if the Prosecution have taken it out with them.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Wladimiroff there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan is out there for the Prosecution. I think they were taking their own Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Wladimiroff there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Hello, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the information here. It is not supported by any ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not take a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I know the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, would you take off your earphones, please? OK, go ahead, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a document here written by the ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- defendant. It is Exhibit 344 which is "My work report for 1990 to 1993".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that the Exhibit, Mr. Niemann, you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. On the English version, Exhibit 344B, the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not supported by any official documentation. It is only the words of the particular person saying he was one of the first members in Prijedor municipality, and no information to say how he would know he was one of the first members in Prijedor municipality. We know that there was a political structure in Prijedor, but nothing that takes it beyond that to say that he was member No. 500 or member 1000 in terms of joining this party. If it is going to be put, perhaps it ought to be put within the context that it arrives, rather than being put in a way that, perhaps, suggests that it comes from some official source which it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is written by the accused himself, your Honour. Obviously, it is the accused himself who can testify as to how he knows about it, but until such time as the accused himself enters the witness box and tells us details of how it is that he comes to know it, we are entitled to put it in cross-examination, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 344 is the work report prepared by Mr. Tadic dated August 8, 1993, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The last sentence of the first full paragraph says: "I saw joining the SDS as my only solution and became one of the first members of the SDS in Prijedor municipality". Your position is that in writing this Mr. Tadic may not have known that he was No. 1, No. 5 or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Stephen has suggested that you put it, Mr. Niemann, to the witness: Did you know that Mr. Tadic has said that he was one of the first members of the SDS in the Prijedor municipality? So I will overrule your objection, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection to that form, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He said that. Of course, it goes to the weight, but he said he was. OK. [To the witness]: Mr. Marro, would you ask Mr. Maric to put his earphones on again, please? Thank you, sir. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware of the fact that Dule Tadic described himself as becoming one of the first members of the SDS in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that he was involved or participated in the organisation of a plebiscite relating to the interests of the SDS in 1991, 1992 -- sorry, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that he held a political position in Kozarac after the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During June or July 1992 did you ever visit Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- the period June/July 1992 did you ever visit Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but it was -- I do not know the date. I went there with a tank driver to get fuel in Omarska. I had never ridden in a tank before and I wanted to see the interior of a tank and to have a ride in it. The driver switched on the tank. I asked him where he was going. He said he was going to Omarska to get fuel. I asked him if I could take a ride with him. So, when we went to Omarska I did not even know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it by virtue of this trip that you are able to ascertain the time it took to get to Omarska and the conditions of the road on the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see, this was before the checkpoint at Orlovci was positioned. I do not understand the question relating to the condition of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you travel to Omarska during June/July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this must have been June, June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Orlovci checkpoint had not been established in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So was the Orlovci checkpoint established in July, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I was not working at the checkpoint at that time, that short period of time. This may have been a question of a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A couple of days in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A couple of days in June when the Orlovci checkpoint was not established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was not working at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did you not say that the checkpoint had not been established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One can interpret this establishment in several ways. The positioning of the police without the container, without the little hut without all the necessary equipment later, and the establishment of a proper checkpoint. So this took some time. When it was established, immediately after its establishment, all the facilities did not exist. These were introduced later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were these facilities introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately how long after the checkpoint was established were the facilities introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry. There is no tone in the earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, we did not hear your last answer. Could you possibly repeat your last answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not pay attention to the time it took to establish the checkpoint and to provide the facilities later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you lived nearby, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry. The interpreter cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would your Honours like to take ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived about four kilometres away from the checkpoint and, apart from working there, I had no connections with the checkpoint. I used a different road to go to town. It is not the same road. I told you there were two roads, an old one and a new one, and I used the old one to go to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we perhaps take the adjournment now?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, was the trip that you took from Orlovci to Omarska in June 1992 in a tank the only trip that you took between Orlovci and Omarska in June and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it the only time or did you travel on another occasion in June/July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you go from Orlovci to Omarska by train? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went there by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to Omarska from some other place by train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went by train from Prijedor to Banja Luka and Sarajevo. I travelled frequently the distance between Prijedor and Sarajevo going through Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is in June and July 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I told you that I never went by train at that time. I never covered the distance Prijedor/Omarska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, there may be some confusion, but I am only asking you to confine yourself to June/July 1992. My first question was when you went by tank in June 1992, was that the one and only trip that you took or did you go on other occasions in June or July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had other occasions to cover the distance Prijedor/Orlovci, Prijedor/Omarska, Prijedor/Banja Luka. I did have other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was in June/July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you travel by train in June/July 1992 from Prijedor to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then how did you get to Omarska in June/July 1992 other than the time that you went there by the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled in a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you travel in a police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once it was a police vehicle, I think, and several times I went in a passenger vehicle to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am only interested in you telling us about when you went to Omarska. Did you go to Omarska on your way to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether you fully understand the notion of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I possibly do not fully understand. Perhaps you might tell me where you went when you went to Omarska in June/July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Prijedor/Banja Luka road, moving from Prijedor, you turn right towards Omarska. It is a settlement, a locality, which is I think about six kilometres from the main road. Are you interested in that locality as such or only the part of the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am interested in both. I am interested in the road that you went to Omarska by and where you went to when you went to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went on a tank, I went to the mine, the Omarska mine, and when I went to Banja Luka, I passed through along the road going to Banja Luka. I did not turn off to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this the only other occasion that you went by the road to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand again. I told you, when you go from Prijedor to Banja Luka you do not pass through the settlement of Omarska. There is a turning leading to that settlement. So there is no need to enter the settlement. Only if you wish to go to the locality of Omarska then you turn off the Prijedor/Banja Luka road to the right to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far is Omarska from the Prijedor to Banja Luka road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, about six kilometres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am concentrating on is your travel from either Prijedor or Orlovci to Omarska during June/July 1992. On one occasion you went by tank. You spoke of two other occasions, one when you went in a private vehicle and one when you went in a police vehicle. When you went in the private vehicle, did you go to Omarska mine again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went in the police vehicle did you go to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to either Omarska mine or Omarska, either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a police vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went in the police vehicle where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that occasion did you go from Orlovci or from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I think I went from Prijedor directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that there may have been other times when you travelled to Omarska in June or July 1992, but you cannot remember precisely those trips now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, there were no other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, you are definite that you only travelled there on two occasions in June/July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that Emir Karabasic was a mutual friend of you and Dule Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that Dule Tadic was a close friend of Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they still close friends in the time that you spoke to Dule Tadic about Emir Karabasic in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Were they still close friends? I know that Dule always spoke about Emir in positive terms and that Emir spoke in positive terms about Dule. They were friends. They were sportsmen. They socialised outside sports as well, and that is how I met them as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you detected no change in their relationship in the year of 1992, I mean, the relationship between Dule Tadic and Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dule Tadic did not say anything to you in July 1992 which suggested that there had been a change in their relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Dule Tadic passed your checkpoint at Orlovci after he had finished working there, when he was going to Kozarac, how was he travelling, by what means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he had a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may not remember this, but could you describe the vehicle that he drove on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot because I saw him a couple of times but in different vehicles. They were different. They were not always the same vehicle. So I could not say whether he owned or drove a single vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you check his papers in the same way as you checked everybody else's papers when they drove to the checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, every vehicle was stopped at the checkpoint, and if you stop the same vehicle or the same persons frequently you necessarily get to know them, so that you do not need to spend more time with that particular driver. So, you stop the vehicle, you look at the papers, you identify the person and then you let them pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So Dule Tadic drove past a sufficient number of times such that you did not need to check his papers on every occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember checking his papers on any occasion when he drove past your checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not, but I think my colleagues working there did once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw your colleagues check his papers as he drove through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that Commander Prpos imposed very strict discipline. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a consequence of imposing this discipline on you, you would have had to follow the orders and directions of the police in Prijedor, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By May 1992, the police in Prijedor had been taken over by the Serb SDS party, the Serb administration, had it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There had been a change in administration from the Muslim administration in Prijedor to the Serb administration in 1992 and by May that change had taken place, had it not, in Prijedor City?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The police were under the control of that administration in May 1992, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that administration had given orders to the police, like you followed orders of your Commander Prpos, the police would have been obliged to follow the orders of the administration as well, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the end of May 1992 the police and civilian authorities were involved in carrying out of ethnic cleansing of Muslims throughout the opstina of Prijedor, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The same police and civilian administrations participated in sending Muslims to camps in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police did not participate in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The police were involved, were they not, in the carrying out of murders and tortures in the camps in the opstina of Prijedor in that period from May through to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, I have had a note from Banja Luka advising me of a number of matters on the transcript that have not come out properly there which I propose to deal with again because they have not been recorded in the same form as here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first matter I want to ask you about ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a little unfair if this is one-sided and we are told that there are difficulties with the transcript in Banja Luka and we are given no such information. I think, in fairness to both parties in these proceedings, if Mr. Marro has difficulties with the transcript in Banja Luka, then it is appropriate that it be passed on to both parties.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I have enquired about the technical facilities. I am told that the transcript that we receive is the same transcript there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it is not different words, but you are saying there have been some errors on the transcript ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- that you wish to correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But it is not that there is a different transcript in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am unable to watch the transcript. What I have received is a fax from Banja Luka pointing out these matters to me. The Prosecution have a lawyer present there as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Certainly. You may clarify questions. I just wanted to assure myself that the transcript that we have here is the same transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am told that it is, but if there are errors in the transcript, then you may clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule your objection on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first matter I want to ask you about

utterances.speaker: MR. MARIC IS THIS
utterances.text: it concerns the place of the checkpoint at Orlovci. The answer recorded was that it was at the "Prijedor/Prijedor road"? Perhaps you would like to re-explain to us where the checkpoint at Orlovci is in relation to the roads between Prijedor and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are moving from Banja Luka, you pass through Kozarac. Then you reach the checkpoint at Orlovci and then you get to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is it on the Prijedor to Banja Luka road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the checkpoint is at the Prijedor to Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next matter I have been asked to clarify with you is if you are travelling from Banja Luka to Prijedor, which side of the road is the tree that you called the walnut tree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are travelling from Banja Luka to Prijedor, it is on the right-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask about those matters. You referred to seeing Dusko Tadic in a motor vehicle after he had finished working at checkpoint Orlovci passing through the checkpoint on a number of occasions. Do you know if he was driving the vehicle he was in or was he a passenger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain because most frequently he was not alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your experience of working at checkpoint Orlovci, if people wished to travel that time between Kozarac and Prijedor and they did not own a vehicle, would they stop vehicles and have a ride by hitchhiking between the two places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population knew that vehicles moving in both directions were being checked at our checkpoint. At that time the traffic was not very heavy, there were no bus connections, there was a shortage of petrol, there was a war going on, so that the local population would be transported with private vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear all of that, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if the answer could be repeated again, Mr. Maric, as we did not hear all of your answer here? I will repeat the question for you, if that is easier. In your experience, having worked at checkpoint Orlovci during this period of 1992, if people were travelling from Kozarac to Prijedor and did not own their own vehicle, did they travel between those two destinations by autostop or hitchhiking and obtaining a lift from a vehicle that was passing along the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us of your ride in the tank to Omarska. Did that tank take you to the site of the iron ore mine outside the village of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were in that tank at the site of the iron ore mine, do you know which part of that place the tank went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It went to the petrol pump to refuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the petrol pump would be placed if you entered the camp by the main gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on the left-hand side. That was the first time I went to the mine and it was the first time I saw the pump station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What other buildings of the site of the mine were in that area where the pump station was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked about other buildings? I did not hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us if there are any other buildings nearby the site of that pump station, and if you know what they are can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are viewing it from the main entrance, to the right is a big building. I think it is for the overhaul or repair of vehicles, of heavy duty trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what distance away from that building is the petrol pump station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, not more than 50, maybe 100 metres. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know the distance from Omarska village of the iron ore mine site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village is divided from the mine by the railway line. So are you thinking of the vehicle repair building or the actual pits? Which part of the mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Take the vehicle repair building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building where vehicles are repaired that I mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is about two kilometres away. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you said you had travelled to Omarska by train when you had taken a train from Prijedor to Banja Luka and to Sarajevo, did you mean that your train had passed through the village of Omarska on its way to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that the checkpoint at Orlovci had existed in different forms. Before the conflict in Kozarac, had there been a checkpoint at Orlovci but in a different form to that in June and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you worked on that checkpoint in its other form before June 1992 or before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see you on the video monitor here and you have no documents in front of you. You were asked about dates of working at checkpoint Orlovci and when it took a particular form. If you had records before you, would that help you in relation to being precise about dates or months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you involved in any way in the activities concerning Muslim people or people from Croatia who were held in camps in the region of opstina Prijedor in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour. We would ask that the witness not be released, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One question, witness, that I wanted to ask you about: you told us about conversations that you had with Mr. Tadic about your mutual friend Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you talk at all to Tadic about where Karabasic was after the conflict, what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is only normal that I asked him because he was a common friend and I asked him whether he knew anything about what had happened to him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you get any answer to that from Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he did not know anything about him and that he did not know what had happened to him during these conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You yourself, did you have any information about what had happened to Karabasic, apart from what Mr. Tadic told you which was nothing really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when did you start at the Orlovci checkpoint? When did you first begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recollect the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it before June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that there are two stages, so to speak, of this Orlovci checkpoint, the stage until the war, until the conflict, broke out and during the time of these conflicts, and the stage when it was -- as it was until the very end, that is to say, with a container and everything else I explained about.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you working at the Orlovci checkpoint when the conflict broke out in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic begin to work at the Orlovci checkpoint after you began to work at the Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he came a bit later, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would your Honour excuse me for a minute?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. We are just checking something on the transcript. Rather than hold the Court up at this stage, your Honour, I would ask that the witness not be released.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you have no further questions? Mr. Maric, you are free to leave now. However, you may be recalled as a witness so you should make yourself available because you may be asked to return again to testify. So, Mr. Wladimiroff is there and you need to keep in touch with him, or he will be in touch with you, if you are asked to come and testify again at that location. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are free to leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay and Mr. Niemann, at some point it would be helpful to the Chamber if you were to write this witness's name in Cyrillic, not you Mr. Wladimiroff, when he returns. I am just asking that it be done because I have looked through the Exhibits trying to find him -- I think it is 66(A), one of the rosters -- some of it is in the Cyrillic alphabet and some is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was looking for his name and could not find it, but if it is in Cyrillic, that is why I could not find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe someone from the translation department.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a good idea, with some approval between the two of you. It does not have to be done today. Someone will do that then. Mr. Marro is there. Would you call your next witness, please, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness to be called by video link, your Honour, is Djuro Prpos. Djuro Prpos, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro would you administer the oath to Mr. Prpos, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you give the Court your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Djuro Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you a serving police officer at Prijedor Police Station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you a Police Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could tell the Court what your rank is now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that superior or inferior to a Police Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a position which is not superior. At present I am Inspector for the co-ordination and monitoring of traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you commence your work as a serving police officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How old are you now, Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you a married man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor or outside Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
